comments.text:
I think if they're just clocking the card faster or slower then it IS the same card, but if they're doing other things like adding or removing cores / stream processors or whatever you want to call them, then it IS a different card or at least a different variation. 
IF you could overclock the older card to match or beat the newer 'higher' model card then it is the same card but if you're missing extra cores I don't think you will be able to do that. 
Or maybe they use faster memory or some components that can handle the overclock more than the old version, then it's technically a different product. 
It's kind of like how Ram works, you can buy higher rated 3200mhz ram but it's pretty much the same thing as 2400mhz, it just costs more because it can achieve a higher speed.

comments.text: Linus get over it, Auto manufacturers re-use the same engine blocks and configurations for not just many products and years, but generations of cars.  Example Corvette mostly the same engine architecture for 60 years.  I understand technology on a micro scale advances alot faster than the macro scale, however,  In my opinion if a GPU is re-used in a "new" product, it's mostly because the GPU was not the bottleneck or was not able to operate at max efficiency/per costs, yada yada.  So redeveloping a Card with an older GPU is no different from Using a Tried and True Engine design in a "new" vehicle.  You get new chips new VRMs and most likely new feature sets, at a more reasonable cost (usually).  Most people can't afford the latest and the greatest anyway and often buy new old stock, which becomes much cheaper when a new "variant" emerges.  Ie: R9 280s going for sub $200 when the 280X came out.

In the last week's WAN show Linus mentioned a misterious product, that he received for review, that the manufactured refused to give any information about, and put Linus under NDA. Despite the fact, that most of that information can be obtained in about 5 seconds by running the appropriate software. He was pissed then already, but couldn't went, because NDA. The product turned out to be 9980XE, with is LITERALLY just better binned 7980XE. Big surprise, big secret release. Yay!
And then, just as he calmed down, the thrid-time-rebranded RX570/580/590 came out.

BAM!

Of course there are many more examples. Radeon 6xxx/7xxx series. Previous GTX rebrands. nVidia's Pascal low end mess of a nomenclature. Intel's mobile same but not even remotely the same nomenclature (I think there is a Pentium and an i7 somewhere in the 3rd get, that literally only differs in clock?). And don't get me satrted about smartphone naming schemes logic.
And so on.

So there you have it.  Not about RX590.

PS: If you spot any information that could be fixed, or clarified better, please let me know and I'll update this post.

comments.text:
I liked when they released the "X" series a few months afterwards with the updated power tuning, and improved board layout, utilizing a slightly refined production process.  

I agree, the 590 should have been a 580X or 580+, or maybe even a 585.  It shouldn't have been called a 590.  

If they wanted to call it a 590, they should have boosted the core count, boosted the memory size, boosted the memory width and/or boosted the cache layout.  Maybe they should have also stitched updated cutting edge Video Encoder/Decoder unit onto the die, instead of relying on the compute based video encoding acceleration that they 580 uses.

Likewise I find the "RTX" series from nVidia misleading, especially since someone BEAT the RTX games to market with a version of Quake 2 that runs real time ray tracing on any GPU that supports Vulkan.   Although, don't expect getting good framerates without a top of the line GPU, so the RTX, being the fastest card on the market at such SSMID compute shaders, to still outshine.

Seriously, if nVidia simply vendor-lock RTX and simply advertised that the nVidia RTX2000 series was optimized for it, they would still sell off the shelves. 

I guess this goes for my two biggest annoyances:   Mislabeled rehash products, and vendor lock "features" misrepresented as hardware features.

First off about the card, pricing and general poor reviews:
I love how almost every reviewer (Linus excluded... I still like you😀) complains about the price of the new RX 590 cards, then goes on to quote the release MSRP price of the AMD Radeon RX 580 4GB blower card of $199.(Linus showed correct launch pricing of entry level 8Gb cards) The MSRP prices of the partner RX 580 8GB cards at launch were $229-$279, and featured much beefier coolers, more fans with all around better cooling, not to mention they were much quieter, and overclocked better. Also AMD is not hiding the fact that these cards are the exact same chip on a improved manufacturing node. While it is fair as a consumer to say the current RX 580 cards are a better value at current price (while they last). This is certainly true. However it is not fair for any reviewer to compare the discontinued stock clearance pricing of RX 580 cards to brand new RX 590 cards and act like they are trying to overcharge the consumer based on new vs clearance. Retailers are discounting hard to get rid of the old discontinued cards, selling them at just above their cost. Also keep in mind that while they still have stock on these older cards, they have no incentive to discount off MSRP on the new models. Also I think a 12% to 15% FPS performance bump is exactly what these RX 590 cards needed to keep pace with newer games and continue to offer solid 1080P 60 FPS at high or ultra settings in most games, which is the market they are intended for. I also think you will see many of these RX 590 cards go on sale for $249 or less in 2019 a after all the RX 580 stock is depleted, and the replacement for Vega at 7nm is looming closer. $20 more ($249 vs $229) is a fair price for the modest performance bump while factoring inflation and the fact that these cards are currently being assessed a 10% Chinese import tariff. Due to the mining crash AMD certainly did not plan on having so many RX 580 & even some RX 570 cards available at the launch of the (new) RX 590. Nvidia is also delaying the launch of the 2060 cards until the stock depletes on the 1060 models, they are just not blowing out the older stock quite as aggressively as AMD. I also would not be surprised if Nvidia just digs a big pit and throws them all away if they still have too many left after Q2 2019. Or maybe they will re brand them as the "NEW" RX 2050 LoL! 😉 At $249 or less in the near future the RX 590 should be a fair market value price for 1080p 60 FPS gaming. @liquidphilosopher1816  
If you're running your PSU so close to its rated limit that you couldn't run a 590, chances are you are losing efficiency and should upgrade anyway [Edit: ESPECIALLY if you're running 24/7!]. Those 80PLUS Bronze, etc ratings are for something like 80% of the rated load. Once you're over 80% of the load, your efficiency plummets and you start drawing 10%, 20% or even more compared to what you are using. 

I would normally ask if you've ever put a meter on the wall side of your system to check its consumption, but as you have a UPS, you should be already able to do this. Compare your system usage to the draw on the wall, and you'll see that you could be saving in the long run by buying a better PSU.

I have a Corsair AX1200W, and although I will never use that much, you can be sure the 10year warranty is a sign of its quality and the 80PLUS Platinum means it offers nothing less than stellar efficiency, especially since I run the thing at roughly 50% utilization, all overclocking considered.

comments.author: @liquidphilosopher1816

comments.text:
@liquidphilosopher1816 
Fair enough. 
When I say efficiency, I don't mean overclock; that's not what I'm talking about. Your powersupply itself has a rated efficiency. At a theoretical 100% efficiency (which is impossible, because science) you will draw the exact same power from the wall that your system requires to run. Good powersupplies are rated as 80PLUS which is 80+% efficient. 

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/80_Plus#Efficiency_level_certifications
If you have a look here, you can see that running a powersupply at 100% of its rated capacity automatically means you get less efficiency than at 50%, which is the point at which a powersupply is most efficient. 

If you are hypothetically running an 80PLUS Bronze at 100%, and you upgraded to an 80PLUS Platinum at double the wattage rating, you will be gaining 10% efficiency. No, this isn't much, and no this is not good advice for everyone, but in your case; running a 400W system at 100% load, with overclocks (meaning you likely have no power saving features enabled), for 24 hours a day, then you would be one of the best examples of someone who would benefit from upgrading; you would save 350 kilowatts per year just by upgrading your power supply [if you aren't already running a good 80PLUS Plat or something].

Furthermore, a more efficient powersupply means your UPS wouldn't struggle as much delivering that power, as a less efficient PSU would consume more power. Your UPS does not need to match your PSU; only your consumption.

Anyway, I hope that's explained well enough.

comments.text: Now Nvidia's RTX 20 series launch makes so much more sense. At first I thought it was a disastrous, botched launch event compared to the impressive Pascal debut, but now it seems Nvidia was actually very skillfully manipulating review sites and the PC hardware press as a calculated advertising strategy. I do wish more corporations who sell products to consumers would just simplify their marketing, pricing, product labeling, and releases a bit. I especially dislike it when PC hardware manufacturers use inconsistent naming schemes for each new generation of a product. For example, the RTX 20 series cards were not labeled exactly the same way as past generations like the 10 series. They should have called the TU102 the RTX 2080 instead of the 2080 Ti, then after a year of refinement of TU102 and possibly a fabrication shrink, optimization, or some other methods to increase efficiency, they should have released an improved version of the 2080 as the 2080 Ti, possibly with 12 to 16 GB of GDDR6 or HBM2 and slightly more CUDA cores and SM's. Coming from a GTX 1080, the RTX 2080 was a really poor value proposition, it even has the same amount of VRAM, albeit slightly faster GDDR6 instead of GDDR5X, but still.

@TheStrangerHAZ  Yeah yeah i know that 14nm finfet  is equal( in size) to 16nm(no finfet) but clock stability is better on the 14nm finfet. All in all  its a very minor difference. GPU Boost 3 is a software feature, that is new to Pascal, and can't be used with Maxwell. Its just software but oc behavior between gpuboost2 and 3 is drastically different. 
With "scaling effects" i meant that Pascal handles temps completly different. Whereas Maxwell just needed enough power and vcore to push high clocks, Pascal will give you high clocks with just lowering the temp. For ex. my 1060 can do 2200Mhz at 1093mv at 37°celsius without any issue.( 5025 time spy graphic score).
As soon as I hit 38°, i'll stick to 2151mhz. 
This behavior is 100% unique to Pascal and was not seen with Maxwell at all. Pascal is more than just Maxwell on steroides, its a (mostly) new architecture.

comments.text:
The biggest disadvantage I see in this re-branding is to to the average, non-tech-savvy consumer. When they buy a computer or laptop, not knowing what they're doing or buying, they typically just go off of the #s on the box. Let's say they know their son wants to play a certain game, and they're buying him a laptop. They look at the back of the game's box and see that it says it needs, for example, an Nvidia GTX1060 or higher. By releasing a WEAKER card under the 1060 moniker later, this may no longer meet the requirements.
It also adds confusion to the relative power levels - again, to the average consumer,  1070>1060>1050 and so on. When you're talking about the average layman buying a PC at Walmart, Best Buy, or somewhere like that, they'll only come in (usually) with a minimal set of information, thinking that so long as they meet that list, they'll be happy with their purchase. Meanwhile, they are generally looking for the cheapest option that meets said requirements. It may not be a good way to shop for PCs, but, having worked for many years in the PC retail industry along with the corporate side of companies and IT department management (ugh, what a stressful job), I can definitely attest to this being the case most of the time. 

Which reminds me... the IT department. Whoever is in charge of ordering new parts for a company. It's WAY way easier to explain to your boss why you paid more for 50x of a part that has a different, higher # on it than one that has the same title. I can see it already... "Well why didn't you just buy THIS brand over here that costs less? It's the same part, right? I mean it has the same model # so that means it's the same thing inside, just order the cheaper one." And then trying to explain to your boss (the company owner, usually) how, again, borrowing the example from earlier, GTX1060>GTX1060=/=GTX1060 nowadays. 
Any proposal that even gets to this point becomes a nightmare for the tech behind it, often slowing things down as they have to justify every large purchase decision. And that's if the CEO doesn't just can the proposal entirely and tell you to start over and hurry up with a more reasonable proposal. (read: cheaper and with higher ROI) because it LOOKS to him like you're spending more on the cards than you could. When you're talking 50-100+ cards, and there's a $100/ea or more difference? It's got to be clear and simple to show in your expense proposals AND reports. Especially the reports, because when you're audited a few years later? It needs to look like you knew what you were doing, and by then who will remember precisely which item is which other old one re-branded how? You don't want it looking like YOU were the wasteful one if the company ever looks for who's costing them too much.

I'm really hoping that AMD's/ATI's pursuits into smaller processes will boost their gaming GPU development and performance in the coming years so that NVIDIA finally has some real competition again.  For the first time in my life I'm gaming on an NVIDIA GPU, and while I must admit that I did lose some of my enthusiasm for ATI when they were taken over/absorbed by AMD (I don't hate AMD or anything, but I do tend to lean towards Intel for the most part on the CPU side; and my personal preference has always been an Intel CPU paired with an ATI GPU in the past), I still love the fact that ATI/AMD are actually trying to push new technology/hardware forward (HBM2 etc.) and I hope that when their next die shrink comes around, they'll have something at least up to the level of a 1080 TI if not a 2080. comments.text: @1BigBen  Actually, at least as I understand it, it's not truly 12NM, it's just that they switched foundries and the 14NM used by the new foundry isn't the same as the 14NM process used by the former, and that's why the claim it's 12NM (I believe it's the same reason that Intel keeps talking about their 10NM being like everyone else's 7NM) and that also explains why the 590 doesn't have as much headroom for overclocking as the 580 does because it's already been overclocked and also why it consumes more power than the 580 out of the box.  Were it truly using a smaller process/transistor size, such optimizations would come naturally without having to increase the power and heat, but the 590 runs hotter and eats up more wattage than its little brother the 580, though they did have to alter the power/PCB to handle that level of power and clock speed, which I believe is where these optimizations came from.  If they'd drop the price or release something that's up to a 1070's level of performance I'd be a lot more excited about the 590, but as it is I'm just kinda meh about it.  It's a decent card with decent performance, but it's not the super value proposition that older ATI/AMD cards were in the past compared to the competition around the same price point/performance level.  Sure, it beats out the 1050/1050 TI, but those aren't really mid-range offerings anyway, and sitting between the 1060 and 1070 but selling for the price that it does really doesn't eliminate NVIDIA from the equation, at least in my opinion.  Had they been able to launch it for around $50+ cheaper, I think it would be much harder to turn down for gamers in the market for a good mid-range GPU, but with the 1060 going for around $200~$225 (at least currently on Newegg) and the 590 going for $280, I don't think it's really worth it for the minor difference in performance on most titles.  I think a lot of people when comparing the two, especially if they research the benchmarks, won't see the value in paying that much more money unless they're really interested in getting those 3 games that come with it (which they won't get until next year anyway, so out of the box they get nothing but the card when they take it home and put it into their PCs).

comments.text:
I have no problem with retunes like the RX590 if they're priced appropriately. (These aren't, IMO. Mining prices have kept MSRPs above where they should be...) 

The main reason being is that unlike most of the G92 rebrands which offered literally nothing new and brought nothing to the table apart from a new name, this still does change things and provide a noticeable benefit and difference despite being the same chip. It's like the HD4890 was back in the day, truly the same chip as its predeccessor (HD4870 in that case) but fixed up enough to warrant a new name and make it generally that bit better. (eg. HD4870 was around 850-900Mhz max core clock when OCing while the HD4890 maxed out around 1Ghz-1.2Ghz depending on cooling and VRM quality) 

As long as they don't go hogwild and start calling the same chip the RX680 next year while launching other chips alongside, I'm okay with it and personally, I actually like these tweak releases because they're honestly the same as when it happens on the CPU field apart from the fact that CPUs tend to have it happen far more often. (eg. Ryzen 1000 and Ryzen 2000, Bulldozer/Piledriver among others provided a small performance increase over their older CPUs and served as a "proof read" version of the design.)

@FlappySock  What are you referring to? Polaris 30 at 1565 MHz can offer same performance per watt as Polaris 20 at 1340 MHz, clocking Polaris 30 to 20 clocks or vice versa would yield huge difference in consumption. Rough estimate would be probably in the 75-100W+ range, as you can cut Polaris 30 consumption down by ~50W by just undervolting it a tad (1.15V > 1.1V, XFX Fatboy variant, didn't affect clocks, other sites have reported similar gains). Running it at Polaris 20 frequencies would lower the consumption just from the clocks already and would allow far lower voltage than what's required at Polaris 30 clocks.

So yes, I would call that vastly.

Resident Evil 2 was promoted with a US$5 million advertising campaign. In Italy, the game reached 100,000 pre-orders, worth over 12 billion lire (about more than 6.6 million dollars).[85] It became the fastest-selling video game in North America. On the weekend following its release, it sold 380,000 copies and grossed US$19 million. It therefore surpassed the revenue of all but one Hollywood movie at that time and broke previous sales records set by the video games Final Fantasy VII and Super Mario 64.[117] With 4.96 million copies sold, the PlayStation version of Resident Evil 2 was a commercial success, and is the franchise's best-selling game on a single platform.[118] Another 810,000 copies of the Dual Shock Ver. were shipped by March 1999.[119] 

The Division: According to Ubisoft, the game broke company records, including highest number of first-day sales[58] (breaking the record previously set by Watch Dogs in 2014), and becoming the company's best-selling game. The Division also broke the industry record for biggest first-week launch for a new game franchise, generating an estimated amount of $330 million globally.[59] The retail version of The Division was the best selling game in its week of release in the U.K. and Ireland, debuting at No. 1 in the UK retail software sales chart. The game's launch marked the biggest video game debut in the first quarter of the year in the U.K., breaking the record previously held by Sony's Gran Turismo 4. It was the third biggest launch of a Ubisoft game in the U.K., behind Assassin's Creed III and Watch Dogs.[60] The game has the highest week one sales for a new intellectual property, breaking the record held by Destiny.[61] The game was No. 1 in Japan, selling over 80,000 units in its first week.[62] The NPD Group indicated that the retail version of The Division was the best selling game in March 2016 in the U.S.[63] 

Capcom expected Devil May Cry 4 to ship 1.8 Million Units by the end of its fiscal year.[76] Upon its release week in Japan, the PlayStation 3 version outsold the Xbox 360 version—140,000 units to 28,000.[77] On February 20, 2008, Capcom's president Haruhiro Tsujimoto announced in a press release that the game shipped two million copies in its first month, making it the fastest selling title in the series.[78] By the end of the title's launch year, it had sold 2.32 million copies and would eventually reach the milestone of three million units sold by December 31, 2014.[79][80] Capcom's Christian Svensson noted the PC retail version's sales in the US did not meet his expectations. A digital download version was only available in pirated form as Capcom Japan did not allow the game to be sold online.[81] A PC digital distribution release was made available over a year later.[82]

comments.text:
Maybe in terms of material only, but it's completely ignorant to think that the price of materials is the only cost they deal with.

I work with plastics injection molding right now, there's a washing machine door handle that we make for an example.  It takes 2 and a half minutes for each part to be made, then we do a second shot of plastic as well that takes about minute to make.  Both tasks have a labor cost as well, overall the labor doubles the cost of production.  Then there's the cost of the machine, maintenance to the machine, cost of a giant metal mold, etc.  And then finally, our company has to make a profit, and then the company that needs these parts has to make a profit, AND retailers have to make profits.  In the end, the cost to you as a consumer can be dollars for an object that only has a few cents worth of plastic in it.  What you didn't see was the hours of labor and all other objects and energy that had to be created and used to make that part.

So instead of looking at the raw materials that you receive, try to think about what it cost to make the raw materials into the useful thing you have.  Otherwise I can just sell you 50 bucks worth of silicon, metals, and plastics and call it a DIY graphics card, have fun making it yourself.

orang I use my computer for work and stuff;
7900x
Dual 1080 TI(s)
Yes 64gigs of ram
With a 500gig m.2 ssd 
1tb ssd 
10tb hardrive 
These are just my specs, I also have their custom loop and it’s really nice to have. With the fans it is a bit loud though because there are purely so many of them... and not really anything I’d switch out.

I actually did switch things around and stuff and they helped me and worked with me on everything. Only thing I’d really advise you with is shipping... I personally had an issue with shipping; so I sent it back and it was fixed and sent back. Because of the 30 day and stuff (yes I have BOTH of their warranties and stuff) which to be completely honestly. Since they worked with me and everything got fixed, and shipping didn’t ruin anything this time (yes because of the issues they upped the shipping to a different one and the crate it comes in is super massive and it is out of wood with foam and stuff on the inside. The only shipping I paid for was the initial one and the return for the fixes thing they paid for and everything as with one of the warranties they pay for the shipping which is a blessing and was worth the value I paid as it’s been used already and the shipping would’ve been more than I already paid for that.)

Other than the shipping issues which was sorta wasted time... I don’t have any complaints. Being able to call and get help if need-be is sorta a simple thing, you can build your own pc... for me, I don’t want to be responsible with (for example) a cpu that’s a thousand bucks... and so-on, plus if anything were to happen instead of getting help manually from the manufacturer and having to do that I just call and I can send it in or whatever. Also, doing a custom loop and stuff I by no means trust myself for something like that.

So I’ve completely enjoyed it for the time I’ve had it. It took awhile with everything, and the shipping issues... so time would be the only issue I’d say. The support is great, for what I’ve experienced and if your pc doesn’t need a custom loop because your using two graphics cards and an oven for a cpu id just advise against it due to noise but temps are absolutely incredible though.
